title: The Home-coming
tagline: Phatik longs for home, is taken to Calcutta, and the home-coming he finally receives is not the one he dreamed of.

overview.intro: Tagore’s “The Home-coming” is a story about homesickness told with the calm inevitability that marks his fiction. Phatik Chakravorti is a hot-tempered village boy — leader of his companions, tyrant to his small brother Makhan, and forever in his mother’s disfavour. When their uncle Bishamber visits from Calcutta, the boy’s behaviour is described to him as one long complaint, and the uncle offers to take Phatik away to be educated with his own children. The city is everything the boy dreamed of until it becomes home to none of his people: neglected, unused to discipline and ailing, he begins to long for his mother and his village with a sickness that no one in Calcutta can read. Published summaries record that the home-coming Phatik finally makes is the one no child should make — he returns to his mother only to be received in death — and the story’s title carries that double edge with unflinching gentleness.

learn.title: Before you read: Tagore’s family stories

blocks.text: Tagore wrote best about what he knew: the joint family of Bengal, its households of mothers and uncles and cousins, and the quiet injuries that affection distributes when it plays favourites. “The Home-coming” belongs to that body of work. As you read, notice two of his habitual instruments. The first is patience with character: nobody in the story is a villain, only a set of people each wrapped in their own concern — a mother absorbed in her favourite, an uncle kindly but partial, a city that cannot hear a boy. The second is the reversal by title: Tagore lets an ordinary phrase carry the whole weight of the ending, so that the last pages reinterpret the first. The story also belongs to a tradition of writing about the Bengali child in Calcutta — educated away from home, lodged with relatives, and tested by a distance that is measured not in miles but in who asks after him. Read it as a story about that distance, and the ending will feel not like a shock but like its completion.

items: Tagore’s subject: the joint family and its quiet distribution of affection.
Nobody is wicked; inattention does the story’s damage.
The title is an instrument: it reinterprets itself at the end.
Home in this story is a person, not a house.

learn.title: The story in outline: the log, the stranger, the city, the return

blocks.text: Published summaries and workbook notes give the story in four movements. First, the village and the log: Phatik and his band of boys plan to roll a heavy log from the river’s mud-flat to annoy its owner, and the game is spoiled when little Makhan — his younger brother, indulged by their mother — walks up and sits on the log, immovable. The boys push at him; Phatik, humiliated before his friends, orders the log rolled with Makhan on it; and when Makhan tells their mother that Phatik has beaten him, Phatik’s temper bursts in front of her. Second, the stranger: at that moment their uncle Bishamber, the mother’s grey-haired brother, arrives from Calcutta on a visit. Hearing his sister’s account of one long tale of mischief, he offers to take Phatik away to be educated with his own children — an offer the boy accepts with wild joy at the thought of the city. Third, Calcutta: the dream curdles. Phatik is a guest in a household that is not his, is lectured for habits no one taught him, neglects his books and grows thinner with each week. His longing for his mother and the village becomes a sickness that his uncle only half reads, until it is clear the boy is seriously ill. Fourth, the return: Phatik is sent home — and the summaries are agreed on the terrible symmetry — the home he reaches at last is not the one he left.

learn.title: The characters: Phatik, Makhan, the mother and the uncle

blocks.text: Phatik is drawn with double vision: to his band he is a captain, quick-tempered and authoritative; at home he is the disappointing son forever compared with his brother. His fault is temper, and his faultlessness is love — the story shows him wrong in the explosion before his mother and right in everything he does for her afterwards. Makhan is the instrument of the household’s injustice: quiet, bookish, pampered, incapable of the mischief attributed to his brother and perfectly capable of the lie that finishes him. The mother rules the household’s affections entirely in Makhan’s favour, and her account of Phatik to the uncle is sincere and unexamined — she is not cruel, only certain. Uncle Bishamber is the well-meaning hinge: he sees a boy ill-used enough to be worth rescuing, and he removes him to a city where, for all his goodwill, nobody in the household can substitute for a mother. Tagore distributes no malice; each character acts from the centre of their own small world, and the story measures the damage that such well-intentioned isolation produces.

items.text: Phatik orders the log rolled with Makhan sitting on it, to save face before his friends.
items.note: Temper and leadership in one gesture — the fault that costs him the village.

items.text: The boy rejoices at the thought of Calcutta before he understands he is leaving his mother.
items.note: The dream begins in excitement and ends in longing.

blocks.text: The second half of the story studies an illness that has no fever: Phatik’s homesickness. Published summaries describe the progression — restlessness, the books he cannot attend to, the thinning frame, the questions about his mother that nobody in Calcutta is placed to answer — and the household reads each symptom as one more failing of a difficult boy. That misreading is Tagore’s point twice over. It shows how easily love is invisible outside its own address: the uncle rescued the body and could not rescue the longing. And it prepares the ending, because the boy’s sickness is measured in units of home, and no physician in the city treats the unit. A careful reading also notices what Tagore refuses to explain: nobody in the story repents loudly, no letter arrives in time, and the mother’s grief is not dramatised as punishment. The story simply completes its arithmetic — a boy far from his mother, an illness nobody names, a journey made too late — and the title, quiet until then, becomes unbearable. The home-coming is delivered, as so often in Tagore, with a gentleness that makes the loss larger rather than smaller.

items: Homesickness appears as restlessness, neglected books and a thinning body.
The household reads each symptom as misbehaviour, not as longing.
The uncle could read the boy’s condition but not its cause.
Tagore refuses melodrama: the ending is arithmetic completed, not punishment announced.
Home, in the story, is a person rather than a place.

learn.title: Themes: home, parental affection and the cost of misjudgement

blocks.text: Home is the first theme and the story’s title: Tagore defines it as wherever a person is wholly known and loved, which is why a boy can be a guest in his uncle’s house for weeks and remain, in the truest sense, homeless. Parental affection and its distribution is the second: the mother’s devotion to Makhan is portrayed without accusation, yet the story shows precisely what such one-sided love produces — a boy who leaves, and a household that reports him wrongly. The misjudgement of Phatik is the third theme: temper is called wickedness, silence is called sulkiness, and love for his mother is never diagnosed at all, because the people who could name it are not listening. Finally, innocence and loss run beneath everything: the story gives Phatik every ordinary boyish fault and then removes him from the only audience that mattered, so that his last journey is measured against the first departure — taken in joy, taken back in vain. Each theme should be anchored in an episode in an answer: the log for temper, the uncle’s offer for misjudgement, the city’s weeks for homesickness, the arrival for the cost.

blocks.caption: Theme and evidence
rows: A guest in Calcutta for weeks, homesick throughout
Temper read as wickedness; longing read as sulkiness
A departure taken in joy, a return too late

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: The events of this story are examined minutely: keep the log incident straight (the plan, Makhan’s sitting, the rolling, the lie told to the mother, the arrival of the uncle), and keep the city movement straight (the neglect, the books, the illness, the decision to send him). Character questions about Phatik should hold both halves — the captain of his band and the judged son — while the mother question must be answered without making her a villain, because Tagore never does. Technique questions ask about the title: prepare to show that it names both the departure from home and the final home-coming, and that the second reading is produced by the ending rather than announced by it. Pathos questions are best answered by restraint — quote the arrangement of events rather than any line, and let the misfortunes speak. As always, this page follows published summaries and workbook notes rather than the text: verify every detail you intend to reproduce in an answer against your own prescribed edition of the story.

questions.prompt: What were Phatik and his friends trying to move when Makhan interfered?
options: A heavy log lying on the mud-flat
A fallen tree branch in the garden
questions.answer: A heavy log lying on the mud-flat
questions.explanation: The boys plan to roll the owner’s heavy log away to anger him, and the game is spoiled when Makhan sits down on it.
questions.commonMistake: The location is the river’s mud-flat, not the house or the fields.

questions.prompt: Who arrives at Phatik’s home at the moment of the quarrel?
options: Bishamber, his mother’s grey-haired brother, from Calcutta
questions.answer: Bishamber, his mother’s grey-haired brother, from Calcutta
questions.explanation: The stranger who arrives at that critical juncture is the mother’s brother from Calcutta, who witnesses the aftermath of the quarrel and offers to take Phatik.
questions.commonMistake: He is the mother’s brother, not the father’s; the connection matters for the household’s respect towards him.

questions.prompt: Why does the uncle take Phatik to Calcutta?
options: He is told the boy is a perpetual nuisance and offers to educate him with his own children
Phatik begs to see the city
The mother insists he be removed
questions.answer: He is told the boy is a perpetual nuisance and offers to educate him with his own children
questions.explanation: Hearing his sister’s account of a lazy, disobedient, wild boy — against a Makhan as good as gold — the kindly uncle offers to take Phatik off her hands and educate him in Calcutta.
questions.commonMistake: The offer begins as relief for the mother, not as a reward for the boy.

questions.prompt: How does Tagore present the mother in the story?
options: As partial to Makhan and severe with Phatik, but not as a villain
As a cruel woman who hates her elder son
As secretly fond of Phatik throughout
questions.answer: As partial to Makhan and severe with Phatik, but not as a villain
questions.explanation: Tagore distributes no malice: the mother’s devotion to Makhan and her complaint about Phatik are sincere, and the story indicts inattention rather than wickedness.
questions.commonMistake: Calling her cruel misreads Tagore’s restraint; she is certain, not evil.

questions.prompt: Phatik’s younger brother, the pampered pet of the household, is named ______.
questions.explanation: Makhan sits on the log, spoils the game and then tells their mother that Phatik beat him — the incident that sets the story moving.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse Makhan with a friend; he is the younger brother.

questions.prompt: How did the boys plan to enjoy themselves at the mud-flat, and what spoiled it?
questions.answer: They planned to roll away the heavy log lying on the mud-flat and so anger its owner for their amusement. Makhan, Phatik’s little brother, sauntered up and sat down on the log without a word; he would not be moved even when pushed, and so spoiled the fun and challenged Phatik’s authority before his companions.
questions.explanation: Both the plan and the interference must be given, because the incident’s whole point is Phatik’s humiliation before his friends.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say Phatik beat Makhan on the mud-flat; the blow happens later, at home.

questions.prompt: How does Phatik’s homesickness show itself in Calcutta?
questions.answer: Published summaries describe a restlessness that the household reads as laziness: he cannot attend to his books, grows thinner week by week, and is forever asking and thinking about his mother and the village. The servants’ scoldings and the lectures of a home that is not his own deepen rather than cure the longing, until the uncle recognises in the boy’s failing health an illness no medicine in the city is treating.
questions.explanation: The symptoms must be tied to their cause, and to the household’s misreading of them, which is Tagore’s central irony.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer merely “he was sad”; the question asks how it showed and how it was misread.

questions.prompt: Trace Phatik’s departure for Calcutta: how it came about and how he received it.
questions.answer: It came about through an accident of temper and timing. The quarrel over the log ends at home with Makhan’s complaint and their mother beating Phatik; at that critical juncture their uncle Bishamber, the mother’s grey-haired brother from Calcutta, arrives on a visit and sees the aftermath. His sister presents her case — one long tale of mischief against a Makhan as good as gold — and the kindly, observant uncle, concluding that the boy is ill-used as much as troublesome, offers to take Phatik to Calcutta and educate him with his own children. Phatik, who had been ashamed before the stranger, receives the offer with wild joy: the city represents escape, and he is impatient to leave. Even his mother’s reluctance, the summaries note, is overborne. The departure is therefore double-edged from the first scene — punishment converted into opportunity, and a home surrendered in excitement before its value is understood.
questions.explanation: The answer sequences cause, offer and reaction, then reads the departure as double-edged, which is the interpretive depth the long answer expects.
questions.commonMistake: Do not present the departure as Phatik’s idea; his joy is a reaction to a decision made for him.

questions.prompt: Why does Tagore call the story “The Home-coming”? Discuss with reference to the ending.
questions.answer: The title names two journeys, and Tagore waits for the ending to complete its meaning. The first journey is a departure from home: Phatik leaves the village in high spirits, and at that moment the words sound like adventure — a boy going out into the world. The second journey is the return, and everything the story has built makes it different: the longing that sickened him, the household that could not read it, the uncle who understood too late. Published summaries record that Phatik returns to his mother only in the final sense the phrase can bear — the home he reaches is not the home he left, because the welcome he dreamed of can never be given. The title therefore becomes an irony of the tenderest and cruellest kind: the boy is indeed home-coming, all the way, and the reader must supply the meaning the family cannot bear to state. Tagore’s restraint — no accusation, no reproach, only the arithmetic of distance, illness and time — is what gives the double sense its force.
questions.explanation: The answer holds both meanings of the title together and shows how the ending produces the second, which is exactly what a title-significance question requires.
questions.commonMistake: Do not paraphrase the ending only; the title itself is the object of the answer.

questions.prompt: Nobody in the story is wicked, yet the tragedy happens. Discuss how misjudgement produces the ending.
questions.answer: The story is a chain of well-intentioned readings, every one of them wrong. The mother reads Phatik as wild and Makhan as golden, and her account to the uncle is sincere — partiality has taught her to see the temper and miss the devotion. The uncle reads the boy as ill-used and rescues him, but rescue without understanding ships the symptom, not the cure: he removes Phatik from the village without asking what in the boy depends on that village. The Calcutta household reads the thinning body and the neglected books as further evidence of a difficult nature, when each is a symptom of a homesickness that nobody names — the uncle half perceives the illness and entirely misses its cause. And Phatik, finally, is misjudged by his own body: the longing that no medicine treats is answered by a journey made after the season for it has passed. Tagore thus distributes no villainy and assigns no blame, because his subject is the machinery of misunderstanding itself — how love can be misread at every address between a village and a city. The tragedy is produced entirely by accuracy failing in small, kind, certain people, and that is why it feels inevitable rather than shocking.
questions.explanation: The answer walks each character’s misreading, shows how each feeds the next, and names the mechanism — the machinery of misunderstanding — rather than hunting for a villain.
questions.commonMistake: Do not blame the mother alone; the question states that nobody is wicked and asks how the tragedy happens anyway.
